title: "No god"
hookLine: the shahada starts with a no: clearing away everything worshiped besides God

lines: A STAR, A MOON, A SUN.
I LOVE NOT THINGS THAT SET.
cards: A night sky, in a story the Qur'an tells about Abraham. He sees a star and says, this is my Lord. The star sets.
Then the moon rises, bright, and he says it again. The moon sets. Then the sun, the biggest yet, and the sun goes down too.

And Abraham says, in Pickthall's translation: "I love not things that set." Before he could turn to the one he called the Creator of the heavens and the earth, he had to let go of everything that rises and falls.
The shahadah opens in the same order.

teach.b: La ilaha. No god. The testimony doesn't start with a yes.
It starts by clearing the ground. First, the word. La is no.

Ilah is a god in the widest sense: whatever is worshiped, whatever a person serves, the thing they give themselves to. So la ilaha is a sweeping no: nothing deserves that. Second, what counts as a god.
In Abraham's day, and in Mecca in the Prophet's day, people bowed to idols of stone and wood. But the Qur'an widens the word on purpose.
Pickthall's translation asks: "Hast thou seen him who chooseth for his god his own lust?" A god there isn't a statue.

teach.h: A GOD CAN BE A WANT THAT RUNS A LIFE.
teach.b: It's a want that runs a life. Some Muslim teachers read this as a warning that money, status, fear, or someone's approval can quietly take that place. Third, why the no comes first.
A yes added to a crowded shelf just becomes one more thing on the shelf.
Clearing comes before choosing: Abraham watched the star, the moon and the sun go down before he turned his face elsewhere. Fourth, read this way, the no isn't a sour word. It frees.

teach.h: A NO THAT SETS A PERSON FREE.
teach.b: If nothing that sets deserves your whole self, then the boss, the screen, the bank balance and the crowd can matter without being in charge. Year three told the long story of people.
Year four begins inside one sentence, and that sentence begins by telling every smaller master: not you.

how: Muslims say la ilaha illallah in prayer and in remembrance, and some teachers explain its opening negation as setting aside anything that competes with God, from idols to money, fame or desire.

o: the testimony's first move: a no to all else worshiped
a claim that God can't be known or described at all
a claim that the world has no maker at all

p: I love not things that set
chooseth for his god his own lust

s: la ilaha is only about statues of stone and wood
the Qur'an speaks of someone who takes his own lust as his god.
the shahadah opens with a negation
la ilaha, no god, comes before the yes.
in the story, Abraham turns away because the star was too small
he turns away from the star, the moon and the sun alike, because they set.

games.q: you are Abraham. the star set, then the moon. now the sun, the biggest light yet, goes down. what do you say?
o: this one was my Lord after all.
I love not things that set.
I'll wait for the star to rise again.
games.why: in Qur'an 6:76–79 he lets go of all of them and turns toward the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

practice: Ask yourself, honestly and without scolding, what gets more of you than it deserves: your phone, someone's opinion, work, worry, a craving.
Don't fight it; name it quietly, the way Abraham named the star, then let it set and rest in the space it leaves. If you pray, you can say la ilaha slowly as you let it go.

wordCard.voice: No god. La ilaha: the shahadah's first move, a no to everything that rises and sets. Today's word.

orig.note: no god: the opening words of la ilaha illallah.

carryVoice: Your line: first, no. Not a sour no, a freeing one. See you tomorrow, for the yes.
